name: Bill Hagerty
bio: Former U.S. Ambassador to Japan and Tennessee Commissioner of Economic and Community Development. Trump-endorsed; $5.3M cash on hand.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Hagerty participated in the Senate Appropriations Committee FY 2026 hearing covering Head Start and childcare funding, which maintained Head Start at FY 2025 enacted levels. His earlier support for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act included quadrupling the employer-provided childcare tax credit. No new Hagerty-specific public statements on early childhood education or pre-K were found in the July 1–6, 2026 window.
early_childhood_ed.details: As a member of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Hagerty participated in Senate Hearing 119-68 (published June 23, 2026) covering FY 2026 appropriations for Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education. The hearing addressed Head Start funding, maintained at the FY 2025 enacted level, and childcare access for working families. The administration's stated priorities for Head Start included expanding parental choice, increasing program efficiency, and promoting parental engagement through faith-based centers. Hagerty's prior legislative record includes voting for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025, which quadrupled the employer-provided childcare tax credit. The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (H.R. 7148) was enacted and published July 1, 2026, covering FY 2026 funding for the Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education, but no Hagerty-specific statements on childcare or early childhood provisions within that legislation were identified. In the July 1–6, 2026 search window, Hagerty's public Senate floor activity focused on DOJ oversight and the CLARITY Act (digital asset legislation); no floor statements, press releases, or public remarks specifically about early childhood education or pre-K were identified.

child_hunger.summary: Hagerty voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025, which cut federal SNAP funding by an estimated $186–$300 billion over a decade. As of June 2026, approximately 100,000 Tennesseans have lost SNAP benefits since the law took effect. A July 2026 federal court ruling voided the USDA's approval of Tennessee's planned SNAP junk-food restrictions, which were set to take effect July 31, 2026. Nationally, a new white paper found SNAP participation has declined by more than 4 million people since H.R. 1 passed, with nearly half of those losing benefits being children. No new Hagerty statements on SNAP or child hunger were found in the July 1–6, 2026 window.
child_hunger.details: The Tennessee Lookout reported on June 16, 2026 that nearly 100,000 Tennesseans have lost SNAP food assistance since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act took effect in July 2025 — a decline from 696,000 recipients in July 2025 to 597,890 in May 2026. The law cut $186 billion from SNAP nationally and expanded work and school requirements, removing prior exemptions for individuals over 55, veterans, and those experiencing homelessness. On June 22, 2026, U.S. District Court Judge Amy Berman Jackson voided the USDA's approval of Tennessee's 'Healthy SNAP Tennessee' pilot program, which would have restricted SNAP recipients from purchasing items listing sugar or corn syrup as the first ingredient starting July 31, 2026; reporting on this ruling continued into early July 2026. A July 1, 2026 white paper from the Center for Science in the Public Interest found that SNAP participation has declined by more than 4 million people nationwide since H.R. 1 passed, with an estimated $187 billion in cuts over the next decade. An Equal Justice Initiative report (July 2, 2026) citing ProPublica analysis found that approximately 776,000 children — nearly half of all those who lost benefits — have lost SNAP access in states with age-specific data. No new statements or actions by Hagerty specifically addressing SNAP or child hunger were identified in the July 1–6, 2026 search window.

parental_support.summary: Hagerty voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in July 2025, which raised the Child Tax Credit from $2,000 to $2,200 per child, made it permanent, and indexed it to inflation. The same law quadrupled the employer-provided childcare tax credit. No new Hagerty-specific statements on paid family leave, parental financial support, or childcare costs were found in the July 1–6, 2026 window.
parental_support.details: Hagerty's primary legislative action on parental financial support remains his July 2025 vote for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. That law permanently raised the Child Tax Credit to $2,200 per child and indexed it to inflation, and it quadrupled the employer-provided childcare tax credit. As a member of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Hagerty participated in FY 2026 appropriations hearings (published June 23, 2026) that addressed childcare access for working families and Head Start funding. Tennessee also saw passage of a state law in spring 2026 requiring immigration status reporting for families receiving state benefits, including the Children's Special Services program for disabled and chronically ill children, affecting approximately 400 families; a Nashville judge on July 2, 2026 extended a temporary restraining order blocking that reporting requirement through at least July 10, 2026. Hagerty made no publicly identified statements on this state-level action during the July 1–6 window. In the same period, Hagerty's Senate floor and public activity focused on DOJ oversight matters and the CLARITY Act (digital asset market structure legislation), with no statements on parental financial support or family policy topics identified.

Memphis-Shelby County Schools and the Mid-South Food Bank distributed groceries to more than 250 Memphis families on July 1, 2026, with District 3 Councilmember Stephanie Love noting that need was greater this summer following Gov.
